Words | Xuhao Du

Editors | Er Mu, Fanyu Meng

Thump… thump… thump-thump. All of us have heard our own heart at some point. When you see someone you like, or after hard exercise, you can hear it beating strong and steady. Beat by beat, it supplies the ammunition for everything we do and keeps us safe. But have you ever wondered where these heart sounds actually come from?

The heart is divided into two parts, the left atrium and the right atrium, and these two atria, together with the muscles that control them, do two all-important jobs: relaxation and contraction. When they relax, they draw blood into the atria; when they contract, they pump it into the blood vessels. This rhythm of relaxing and contracting keeps the blood flowing.

Throughout the cycle, four important valves control which way the blood flows: the tricuspid valve, the mitral valve and the two semilunar valves. The heartbeat we normally hear is these four valves each snapping shut, slap, slap, slap: the sound of the leaflets meeting as each valve closes. Normal blood flow is laminar, so it makes no sound.

Let’s go back to the phonocardiogram shown in the previous article, The body’s symphony, part 1: the sound of a heartbeat:

Figure 1. Phonocardiogram

This time we’ll take each sound apart and line it up with the blood flow to see at which stage it is produced. To help explain, Figure 2 is a simplified cross-section of the heart showing the four valves:

Figure 2. Cross-section of the heart (hand-drawn by the author’s spouse)

First, blood flows from the blood vessels into the atria. At this point the tricuspid and mitral valves both open; once the atria have filled with blood, the tricuspid and mitral valves both close, producing the first heart sound, S1. So the first heart sound is actually two sounds combined, but because they happen almost simultaneously, we can basically only make out one.

Then, when the atria contract, the semilunar valves open to let blood flow into the blood vessels; once all the blood has left the atria, both semilunar valves close, producing the second heart sound, S2. So, again, the second heart sound is made up of two sounds. These two are less well synchronized than the two in the first heart sound, so they can be told apart to some extent.

So how can heart sounds reveal heart disease? Mainly through two features: picking up abnormal heart sounds and where they are picked up.

Take the fourth heart sound, S4. It is usually produced during atrial contraction, when the tissue around the atria is under tension, and it generally appears about 0.1 s before S1, that is, late in diastole. One pathological cause of S4 is blood being forced into the atrium by pressure overload.

Murmurs are another major source of abnormal heart sounds. They are caused mainly by turbulence, which can result from valve disease (a deformed valve, or one that does not close fully), from abnormal blood flow caused by disease of the atria, and so on. By picking up a murmur and locating where it occurs, a doctor can to some extent tell what kind of heart problem is involved, which helps with initial diagnosis and treatment.

Finally, judging the health of your heart by its sounds is a complex, system-level undertaking, and nothing in this article should be used to diagnose disease. If you feel unwell, remember to see a doctor! Below are recordings and waveforms of some abnormal heart sounds, along with the conditions behind them.
